body:
Why Heating Water Produces Circulation

Consider water being heated from below in a vessel. The water close to the heated surface becomes warmer first.

As it warms, its density generally decreases, provided the water is above approximately 4°C. The warmer, less dense water tends to rise, while cooler and denser water moves downward to replace it.

This movement creates circulation within the water. Heat is transported from one region to another by the moving fluid.

Convection is the transfer of heat through the bulk movement of a fluid, such as a liquid or gas.

Unlike conduction, convection involves the movement of the substance carrying thermal energy.

Why Convection Occurs Mainly in Fluids

Liquids and gases can flow, allowing warmer and cooler portions to move relative to one another. Ordinary solids do not flow in this manner and therefore do not generally transport heat through bulk convection.

In a heated fluid, density differences can produce movement under gravity. This is called natural convection.

Fluid movement can also be produced by external devices such as fans and pumps. Heat transfer involving such movement is called forced convection.

For example, a fan helps move air across a warm surface, allowing heat to be carried away more rapidly. The fan does not itself make the air colder merely by moving it.

Convection in Air

Air heated near a warm surface generally becomes less dense and rises. Cooler surrounding air moves in to replace it.

This is why warm air commonly rises above a heater and why rising air currents can form above strongly heated ground.

The process is also important in atmospheric circulation, although actual wind patterns depend on pressure differences, terrain and other weather conditions.

Sea Breeze: During the Day

Land generally heats more rapidly than the sea during the daytime because water has a high specific heat capacity and distributes absorbed heat through a considerable depth.

As the land becomes warmer, the air immediately above it heats up and tends to rise. A pressure difference can then develop, causing relatively cooler air from the sea to move towards the land near the surface.

This movement is called a sea breeze.

At higher levels, a compensating movement may carry air back towards the sea, completing a circulation pattern.

Land Breeze: During the Night

At night, land generally loses heat more rapidly than the sea. Consequently, the air above the land often becomes cooler than the air above the nearby sea.

Under suitable conditions, relatively warmer air rises above the sea and cooler air moves from the land towards the sea near the surface.

This movement is called a land breeze.

FeatureSea breezeLand breeze
Typical occurrenceDaytimeNighttime
Relatively warmer surfaceLandSea
Near-surface wind directionSea towards landLand towards sea
Main causeDifferential daytime heatingDifferential nighttime cooling

Sea breezes and land breezes are typical local circulation patterns, not winds that must occur in the stated direction every day. Strong prevailing winds and local weather conditions can weaken or alter them.

Connection with Gujarat

Gujarat has an extensive coastline along the Arabian Sea, including coastal areas around Kachchh and Saurashtra.

The same differential heating and cooling principles can produce local sea-breeze and land-breeze circulations along suitable parts of this coastline.

The general physics is the same as on other coasts: differences between the heating and cooling rates of land and water influence the temperature and pressure of the surrounding air.

This relationship connects specific heat capacity, convection and local coastal winds.

Prelims focus

  • Convection involves the movement of a fluid.
  • In ordinary natural convection, warmer and less dense fluid tends to rise.
  • Natural convection is driven by buoyancy associated with density differences.
  • During the day, a sea breeze typically blows from sea towards land.
  • During the night, a land breeze typically blows from land towards sea.
  • Trap: The direction of the near-surface breeze is different from the compensating movement of air at higher levels.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4: Heat, section 4.4, printed pp. 41–43, 2018–19 printing; U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School, Specific Heat Capacity and Water, 24 August 2026, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Convection: Heat Transfer in Liquids, Gases and Coastal Winds

body:
How Heat Reaches Earth from the Sun

Heat from the Sun reaches Earth across the near-vacuum of space. Since conduction and convection require matter, they cannot explain this transfer across empty space.

The transfer occurs through radiation.

Thermal radiation is the transfer of energy through electromagnetic waves emitted by matter because of its temperature. Unlike conduction and convection, radiation does not require a material medium.

All objects at temperatures above absolute zero emit thermal radiation. Hotter objects generally emit radiant energy at a greater rate than cooler objects of otherwise comparable properties.

Infrared radiation is particularly important in many everyday heating situations. The Sun also emits visible light and other electromagnetic radiation.

Absorption, Reflection and Transmission

When radiation strikes a surface, some may be absorbed, some reflected and, depending on the material, some transmitted through it.

The absorbed portion increases the energy of the receiving object.

The following school-level observations are useful:

  • Dark, dull surfaces: Generally absorb a greater proportion of incident visible sunlight than light-coloured surfaces of similar material.
  • Light-coloured surfaces: Generally reflect a greater proportion of visible sunlight.
  • Highly polished metallic surfaces: Often reflect thermal radiation effectively and have relatively low thermal emissivity.

Actual radiation absorption and emission depend on wavelength and surface properties, not merely on the colour visible to the human eye.

Why Light-Coloured Clothing Is Often Preferred in Summer

Light-coloured clothing generally reflects more incident sunlight than otherwise similar dark clothing. This can reduce solar heating of the clothing.

However, comfort also depends on fabric thickness, ventilation, humidity and the ability of sweat to evaporate.

Therefore, clothing colour is one factor affecting thermal comfort, not the only factor.

Thermal Insulation

Thermal insulation involves reducing unwanted heat transfer between regions at different temperatures.

Insulation is useful both for keeping warm objects warm and for keeping cool objects cool.

For example, an insulated water container loses heat more slowly when filled with hot water and gains heat more slowly when filled with cold water.

Why Woollen Clothes Keep Us Warm

Woollen fabrics contain numerous small spaces that trap air. Air is a poor conductor of heat, and restricting its movement also reduces convection.

Consequently, heat escapes from the body more slowly.

A woollen sweater does not continuously produce heat. It reduces the rate at which the body loses heat to colder surroundings.

Several clothing layers may be effective because the layers trap additional relatively still air.

How a Vacuum Flask Reduces Heat Transfer

A vacuum flask is designed to reduce the transfer of heat between its contents and the surrounding environment.

Its insulating effect results from several features.

  • Evacuated space: The low-pressure gap between the inner and outer walls greatly reduces conduction through gas and prevents ordinary convection across that gap.
  • Reflective surfaces: Shiny or reflective surfaces reduce the exchange of thermal radiation.
  • Insulating stopper: A properly fitted stopper reduces heat transfer and limits the escape of vapour.
  • Limited contact between walls: Suitable supporting structures reduce conduction through solid connections.

No ordinary vacuum flask eliminates heat transfer completely. Some energy can still pass through its stopper, supports and other parts.

Insulation in Buildings

Buildings can reduce heat gain during summer and heat loss during winter by using insulating roofs, walls and other suitable construction materials.

Hollow bricks and materials containing trapped air can slow heat transfer. A ventilated air space can behave differently from a sealed air space because moving air may carry heat by convection.

Reflective roof surfaces can reduce the absorption of sunlight, while insulation slows heat flow through the building envelope.

These principles are relevant in hot regions of Gujarat, where reducing unwanted heat gain can lower the demand for indoor cooling.

Comparing All 3 Modes of Heat Transfer

ModeEssential mechanismMaterial mediumTypical example
ConductionEnergy transfer through interactions within or between materialsRequiredMetal spoon heating in tea
ConvectionMovement of fluid carrying thermal energyRequiredCirculation of heated water
RadiationElectromagnetic energy transferNot requiredSolar energy reaching Earth

Prelims focus

  • Radiation can transfer heat through a vacuum.
  • Solar energy reaches Earth through electromagnetic radiation.
  • Shiny metallic surfaces are generally effective reflectors of thermal radiation.
  • Woollen clothing reduces heat loss partly by trapping air.
  • A vacuum flask reduces multiple modes of heat transfer.
  • Trap: A vacuum reduces conduction and convection across its gap, but it does not prevent radiation.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4: Heat, sections 4.4–4.5, printed pp. 42–45, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Radiation and Thermal Insulation: Controlling Heat Transfer

body:
What Happens to Matter When Heated?

Most substances expand when their temperature increases and contract when their temperature decreases, provided other relevant conditions remain suitable.

This change in dimensions is called thermal expansion.

Thermal expansion is the increase in the dimensions or volume of a substance caused by an increase in temperature, under specified physical conditions.

When a substance is heated, its particles generally move or vibrate more vigorously. Changes in their average separation can cause the substance to occupy more space.

Thermal expansion does not mean that the individual atoms necessarily become larger.

Expansion in Solids, Liquids and Gases

Solids, liquids and gases can all exhibit thermal expansion, but their behaviour differs.

Solids

Solid objects commonly expand in length, area and volume when heated.

Examples include the increase in length of a metal rod and the increase in diameter of a heated metal ring.

The dimensions usually decrease again when the object cools, provided it has not undergone permanent deformation or another irreversible change.

Liquids

Most liquids increase in volume when heated over their ordinary temperature ranges.

Traditional liquid-in-glass thermometers use this property: the level of the liquid changes as temperature changes.

Gases

Gases can show substantial expansion when heated if they are free to expand against approximately constant external pressure.

For example, air in a flexible balloon can occupy a larger volume when heated.

If a gas is enclosed in a rigid sealed container, its volume cannot increase appreciably. Heating then generally increases its pressure instead.

For comparable temperature changes under suitable conditions, gases generally show much greater fractional expansion than solids. The exact expansion depends on the substance and the conditions under which it is heated.

Practical Applications of Expansion

Fixing Metal Rings on Wooden Handles

A metal ring intended to fit tightly around a wooden handle may initially be too small to slide into position.

Heating expands the ring, increasing its internal diameter. The wooden handle can then be fitted into place.

As the ring cools, it contracts and grips the handle more tightly.

The same principle has traditionally been used to fit metal rims around wooden cart wheels.

Railway Tracks and Bridges

Metal structures change dimensions with temperature. Railway tracks and bridges must therefore be constructed so that temperature-related movement can be accommodated safely.

Expansion joints or other engineering arrangements may be used for this purpose.

It is incorrect to assume that every modern railway track must have a visible open gap between successive rail sections. Continuously welded tracks can accommodate thermal effects through other arrangements.

Bimetallic Strips

A bimetallic strip consists of 2 bonded metals that expand by different amounts for the same temperature increase.

On heating, the strip bends towards the metal having the smaller thermal expansion, assuming ordinary conditions and appropriate strip construction.

This behaviour is used in certain temperature-responsive switches and thermostats.

The Special Behaviour of Water

Most liquids contract when cooled, but pure water exhibits an important exception near its freezing point.

At ordinary atmospheric pressure, liquid water has its maximum density at approximately 4°C.

When water is cooled from temperatures above 4°C towards 4°C, its volume decreases and its density increases.

When water is cooled further from 4°C towards 0°C, it behaves differently: its volume increases and its density decreases.

This unusual behaviour is called the anomalous expansion of water.

Why Ice Floats on Water

During freezing, water molecules form an open crystalline arrangement. This structure occupies more volume than the same mass of liquid water.

Consequently, ordinary ice is less dense than liquid water and floats on it.

This differs from the behaviour of many substances, whose solid forms are denser than their liquid forms.

Importance in Lakes and Ponds

In sufficiently cold conditions, surface water cools and becomes denser until it approaches 4°C. This denser water can sink.

Further cooling below approximately 4°C produces less dense water, which tends to remain near the surface. Ice can eventually form on top.

The floating ice layer slows further heat loss from the water below. This helps aquatic organisms survive beneath ice in cold climates.

The phenomenon is especially important for freshwater bodies in regions experiencing freezing winters.

Prelims focus

  • Most substances expand on heating and contract on cooling.
  • Thermal expansion explains the fitting of heated metal rings.
  • Bimetallic strips use the unequal thermal expansion of 2 metals.
  • Pure water has maximum density at approximately 4°C.
  • Ordinary ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
  • Trap: Between 0°C and 4°C, liquid water contracts on heating instead of expanding.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 6: Changes Around Us, printed pp. 48–50, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 1: Matter in Our Surroundings, printed pp. 4–8, 2018–19 printing; U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School, Water Density, 24 August 2026, consulted 3 November 2026.]
